summary: Hebrew numbers the days of the week from Sunday: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן “first day” (Sunday), יוֹם שֵׁנִי “second day” (Monday) … יוֹם שִׁשִּׁי “sixth day” (Friday); only the seventh has a name, שַׁבָּת. In Israel the week starts on Sunday and the weekend (סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ) is Friday and Saturday. Telling the day needs no verb in the present: הַיּוֹם יוֹם שֵׁנִי “today (is) Monday”, מָחָר שַׁבָּת; in the past it takes הָיָה / הָיְתָה: אֶתְמוֹל הָיָה יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן. “On Monday” is בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי (no article). The parts of the day take בְּ with the article — בַּבֹּקֶר “in the morning”, בַּצָּהֳרַיִם “at noon”, בָּעֶרֶב “in the evening”, בַּלַּיְלָה “at night” — except אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם “in the afternoon”, which needs nothing. With the article alone they mean “this …”: הַבֹּקֶר “this morning”, הָעֶרֶב “this evening”, הַלַּיְלָה “tonight” — and הַיּוֹם, “the day”, is “today”. Words of time (הַיּוֹם, מָחָר, עַכְשָׁו, בַּבֹּקֶר …) usually open the sentence or close it; frequency words (תָּמִיד, לִפְעָמִים, לְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת) stand before the verb or at the start, and “never” is אַף פַּעַם + לֹא. With מָחָר the present is enough for a plan: מָחָר אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ. Hebrew verbs have no aspect: “I am going” and “I go” are the same form.

blocks.caption: Frequency words stand before the verb or open the sentence.

blocks.title: No verb, no article
blocks.text: “Today is Monday” = הַיּוֹם יוֹם שֵׁנִי — no “is”. “On Monday” = בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי — no article (בַּיּוֹם הַשֵּׁנִי would be “on the second day”).

blocks.title: Sunday is a working day
blocks.text: In Israel the week starts on יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן; the weekend is Friday and Saturday. “See you after the weekend” means Sunday.

blocks.title: Yesterday needs the past
blocks.text: אֶתְמוֹל goes with a past verb: אֶתְמוֹל הָיָה יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן “yesterday was Sunday”, אֶתְמוֹל הָיְתָה שַׁבָּת (שַׁבָּת is feminine). The past tense comes in lesson C01.

blocks.title: For you
blocks.text: German says am Montag, morgens, heute Abend — Hebrew בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, בַּבֹּקֶר, הָעֶרֶב. Greek numbers the weekdays like Hebrew (Δευτέρα, Τρίτη, Τετάρτη, Πέμπτη); Russian counts from Monday (вторник “second” is Tuesday) — Hebrew counts from Sunday. Turkish and German put the time word early, as Hebrew may: Yarın Hayfa’ya gidiyorum / Morgen fahre ich nach Haifa / מָחָר אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ לְחֵיפָה.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is it the name of a day? → (בְּ)יוֹם + ordinal; Saturday = שַׁבָּת.
A part of the day: “in the …” (בַּבֹּקֶר) or “this …” (הַבֹּקֶר)?
How often? → תָּמִיד / לְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת / לִפְעָמִים / אַף פַּעַם לֹא.

askYourself: Am I naming the day? → הַיּוֹם / מָחָר + the day, no verb: הַיּוֹם יוֹם שֵׁנִי. Yesterday → אֶתְמוֹל הָיָה …
Is it “on (a day)”? → בְּיוֹם … (no article); Saturday → בְּשַׁבָּת.
Is it “in the morning / evening / at night”? → בְּ + article: בַּבֹּקֶר, בָּעֶרֶב, בַּלַּיְלָה; “in the afternoon” → אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם.
Is it “this morning / this evening / tonight”? → the article alone: הַבֹּקֶר, הָעֶרֶב, הַלַּיְלָה.
How often? → תָּמִיד, לְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת, לִפְעָמִים before the verb; never → אַף פַּעַם … לֹא.
Every …? → כָּל + noun without article: כָּל יוֹם, כָּל בֹּקֶר.
steps: Add בְּ or the article as needed.
Put it at the start (or the end) of the sentence; frequency words before the verb.

traps: Monday is יוֹם שֵׁנִי “the second day” — not the first.
*בְּבֹקֶר → בַּבֹּקֶר (the parts of the day take the article).
הָעֶרֶב is “this evening”, בָּעֶרֶב “in the evening” — one vowel apart.
“Never” needs לֹא too: אַף פַּעַם לֹא.
מְאֻחָר is “late” (adverb); “he is late” is הוּא מְאַחֵר.

quiz.why: The week counts from Sunday (יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן): the second day is Monday.

quiz.q: “In the morning I drink coffee” (a man):
quiz.why: The parts of the day take בְּ + the article: בַּבֹּקֶר.
The article alone means “this”: הָעֶרֶב, הַבֹּקֶר, הַלַּיְלָה.
No verb in the present and no preposition.

quiz.q: Which days make the Israeli weekend?
quiz.why: The week starts on Sunday (יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן); סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ is Friday and Shabbat.

options: הוּא אַף פַּעַם לֹא בָּא מֻקְדָּם.
quiz.answer: הוּא אַף פַּעַם לֹא בָּא מֻקְדָּם.
quiz.why: אַף פַּעַם “ever” needs לֹא to mean “never”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic also counts the days from Sunday — الْأَحَد “one”, الْإِثْنَيْن “two” … الْخَمِيس “five” — and calls Friday الْجُمُعَة and Saturday السَّبْت (= שַׁבָּת).
German am Montag, am Morgen / morgens, heute Abend: a preposition with a case where Hebrew uses בְּ or just the article (בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, בַּבֹּקֶר, הָעֶרֶב).
Chinese counts from Monday (星期一 = Monday) and puts the time word before the verb; Hebrew counts from Sunday and is free to put it first or last.
Chinese marks completed or experienced actions with 了 / 过 in this lesson; Hebrew verbs have tense, not aspect — the past comes later (C01).
